metaTitle: 6 Best Dish Soap Dispensers for the Sink (2026)
metaDescription: Six dish soap dispensers compared for sink-side use: weighted steel, sponge caddy pumps, glass pairs and a touchless option, with who each one suits.
introParagraphs: A dish soap dispenser lives in the busiest corner of the kitchen, so small design choices show up dozens of times a day. A pump that tips over when you press it, a bottle that is too narrow to refill without spilling, or a neck that lets soap crawl down the outside will annoy you far more than a bottle that simply looks plain. This guide compares six sink-side dispensers that were chosen because they handle dish soap or hand and dish soap duty in a kitchen, not because they were the cheapest bottle on the shelf.

The lineup covers a real spread. The OXO Good Grips Stainless Steel Soap Dispenser is a weighted, non-slip steel pump built for one-handed use. The LIFEEZY and Casabella Sink Sider Solo both fold a sponge caddy into the same footprint as the pump, which saves counter space around the faucet. The COHOSEGE 16 Oz glass set and the JASAI 18 Oz glass 2-pack give you two matched bottles so hand soap and dish soap never get swapped, and the PZOTRUF 17 Oz is the one touchless model, using an infrared sensor with five output settings.

We evaluated each pick from its listing, specs and buyer feedback rather than claiming hands-on testing. For every dispenser we looked at capacity, pump behavior, how stable the base is when you press down, how easy the opening makes refilling, and what the material means for a wet, soapy environment. The sections below explain what each one does well, where it falls short, and which kind of kitchen it fits.

products.name: OXO Good Grips Stainless Steel Soap Dispenser
products.description:
The OXO Good Grips Stainless Steel Soap Dispenser is the simplest answer to the most common dish soap problem, which is a bottle that slides or tips when you press the pump. The base is weighted and has a non-slip surface, so you can press down with a wet hand and the body stays where it is. The listing describes it as designed for busy cooks who want to dispense one-handed, and that framing fits: your other hand can keep holding a pot or a sponge.

The pump head is soft and cushioned, which makes repeated pressing gentler on the palm during a long cleanup after a family meal. Stainless steel is rust-resistant and does not show scratches the way clear plastic does, though a steel body hides how much soap is left, so you will learn to judge by weight or by lifting the pump out. Compared with the glass pair from COHOSEGE, the OXO is much harder to break if it gets knocked into the sink.

In ownership terms this is a no-fuss tool. You wipe the outside with a damp cloth, top it up when the pump starts to sound dry, and otherwise leave it alone. It does not include a sponge holder like the Casabella Sink Sider Solo, so if you want a scrubber parked beside it you will need a separate dish. It also has no sensor, so it never needs batteries, which puts it ahead of the PZOTRUF for people who prefer fewer things to maintain.
products.bestFor: Anyone who wants a sturdy, weighted pump that stays put and needs no batteries.

products.name: LIFEEZY Dish Soap Dispenser with Caddy
products.description:
The LIFEEZY combines a dish soap pump with an attached caddy that the listing says holds sponges, scrubbers and rags. The idea is to cut down on the number of separate objects around the faucet, so one footprint does the work of a bottle plus a dish. At 13 ounces it holds less than the 17 ounce PZOTRUF or the 16 ounce COHOSEGE bottles, which is the main trade for the all-in-one layout.

The listing pitches it as a way to spend less time at the sink and eliminate the mess of soap dripping down the outside. A caddy that sits right under the pump does help with the second part, because any drips land near a place where a sponge can soak them up. The sponge dries in open air beside the pump instead of sitting wet in a puddle on the counter, which is a small hygiene win for anyone who has dealt with a slimy sponge dish.

Ownership is straightforward but a little more fiddly than a bare bottle. You will wipe the caddy area now and then because soap residue gathers where wet sponges rest. Next to the Casabella Sink Sider Solo, which also pairs a pump with a caddy and ships with a sponge included, the LIFEEZY is the pick when you want a larger sponge shelf and care less about getting a starter sponge in the box.

products.name: Casabella Sink Sider Solo Soap Pump and Sponge Caddy
products.description:
The Casabella Sink Sider Solo is a two-in-one: a soap pump with a sponge caddy built into the same body, and the listing says a sponge comes in the box. You press the pump so soap lands directly on the sponge that is already sitting beside it, which is a neat shortcut when you are washing a few dishes and want to skip the step of squeezing soap from a bottle. The white and chrome look blends into most kitchens without drawing attention.

Refilling is where it stands out against the other caddy pick. The listing says you pull the tab up to remove the pump, then pour soap into a wide-opening bottle. A wide mouth means a funnel is rarely needed, which matters for anyone pouring from a large refill jug with a shaky or tired wrist. It works with hand soap or dish soap, so it can serve either side of a sink.

The tradeoff is that the design is compact, and you do not get the bottle volume of the 18 ounce JASAI glass bottles. The sponge sitting in the caddy also needs replacing on a schedule, since a sponge kept in a damp spot ages quickly. Against the LIFEEZY, the Casabella is the more finished, polished product to look at, while the LIFEEZY leans toward being a utilitarian holder for several scrubbing tools.
products.bestFor: People who want a tidy pump with a sponge included and easy refills.

products.name: COHOSEGE 16 Oz Glass Soap Dispenser Set
products.description:
The COHOSEGE set gives you two glass dispensers with labels for hand soap and dish soap, which solves a real kitchen problem: reaching for the wrong bottle with wet hands. The pair is meant to be read at a glance, so one stays at the sink for dishes and the other covers hand washing. The listing leans on a modern farmhouse look, and glass with a white pump reads as décor rather than a utility item.

Each bottle holds 16 ounces, which is a comfortable middle: bigger than the 13 ounce LIFEEZY but a little under the 18 ounce JASAI glass bottles. Glass lets you see the soap level and the soap color, and it will not take on stains or a plastic smell. The cost of that clarity is weight and fragility. A glass bottle on a wet sink edge can slip, so it is worth keeping it away from the very rim.

Daily life with this set is easy as long as you respect the glass. Rinse and refill when the pump begins to gasp, and keep the labels clean so they stay readable. Compared with the JASAI 2-pack, the COHOSEGE gives you labels so you do not guess which is which, while the JASAI gives you a larger bottle and a stainless steel pump. If you want the sturdiest option, the OXO steel pump is a safer choice for households with kids or a slippery counter.
products.bestFor: Kitchens that want matched glass bottles with clear hand and dish labels.

products.name: JASAI 2-Pack 18 Oz Glass Soap Dispenser
products.description:
The JASAI 2-pack offers two 18 ounce glass bottles with a rust-proof 304 stainless steel pump, and the listing says they hold soap, lotion, hand soap and dish soap. That makes this the largest capacity in a matched pair here, so you refill less often than with the 16 ounce COHOSEGE bottles. Thick glass and a metal pump head give the pair a sturdier feel than many bargain bottles.

The blank wooden tag is a small touch with real use. You can write dish or hand on the tag, which does the same job as printed labels, only in your own handwriting and with the option of changing it later. Two bottles also work well if you keep one at the kitchen sink and move the other to a bathroom or laundry room, rather than treating them as a strict pair.

Expect the usual glass tradeoffs: more weight and a smooth surface that is slippery when soapy. A stainless steel pump resists corrosion in a damp kitchen, which is a strength over a plain plastic pump that can crust over. Compared with the OXO, you give up the weighted non-slip base but gain visibility and volume. Against the Casabella, you lose the built-in sponge caddy but gain far more soap capacity, so the choice comes down to whether you value storage space or stand-alone volume.

products.name: PZOTRUF 17 Oz Automatic Touchless Dispenser
products.description:
The PZOTRUF 17 Oz is the only touchless dispenser in this comparison. An infrared sensor detects a hand within a couple of inches and releases soap with no press required, which is useful when your hands are covered with raw chicken, dough or grease and you do not want to touch a pump. It holds 17 ounces and has a wide opening, which makes refilling less of a balancing act than narrow-necked bottles.

Five adjustable output levels let you choose how much soap each trigger delivers. A low setting suits thin dish soap and keeps waste down, while a higher setting suits thicker liquids. That control is a real advantage over fixed-dose manual pumps, though it adds a menu of options that a user who only wants one press may not care about.

The cost of touchless is upkeep. It needs a power source, so you should check the battery or charging detail on the listing before buying, and a sensor can misfire if the soap is very thick or the cell is running low. Compared with the OXO, the PZOTRUF takes more attention but removes the pumping motion entirely. If you have trouble pressing a pump repeatedly, this is the model to choose, and if you prefer fewer parts that can fail, the OXO or the Casabella is the calmer option.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A dish soap dispenser gets pressed with wet, slippery hands, so a light bottle often slides or tips. Look for a weighted base or a non-slip pad, because those features keep the unit in place when you push down on the pump. In this lineup the OXO Good Grips Stainless Steel Soap Dispenser is the one built around this idea, with a weighted, non-slip base. Glass options like the JASAI 18 Oz pair feel heavy once filled, but a smooth glass bottom can still skate on a wet counter, so a mat or a spot away from the sink rim helps.

Capacity sets how often you refill, and refilling is the task most people dislike. A dish soap bottle that holds 13 ounces, like the LIFEEZY, will need topping up sooner than the 16 ounce COHOSEGE bottles or the 18 ounce JASAI pair. The 17 ounce PZOTRUF sits between them. Heavy daily dishwashing in a family of four justifies the larger sizes, while one or two people can live happily with a smaller reservoir that takes up less counter space.

A narrow neck turns each refill into a spill, especially when you pour from a big jug of dish soap. A wide opening lets you pour directly or use a short funnel. The Casabella Sink Sider Solo is described as having a wide-opening bottle with a pull tab to remove the pump, and the PZOTRUF 17 Oz is also described with a wide opening. If you refill from a gallon container, prefer these over narrow bottles, and always pour slowly so thick soap does not trap air in the pump.

Kitchens are wet, soapy and occasionally clumsy, so material matters more than looks. Stainless steel resists rust and survives drops, which is why the OXO makes sense for a busy household. Glass, as on the COHOSEGE and JASAI sets, is easy to see through and does not stain, but it can crack against a faucet or the sink edge. The JASAI also uses a 304 stainless steel pump, which resists corrosion better than a basic plastic pump head that may crust or seize with age.

Counter space around a sink is tight, and a separate sponge dish adds clutter. Combined units like the LIFEEZY and the Casabella Sink Sider Solo put a sponge next to the pump, so soap and scrubber share one footprint. The Casabella includes a sponge and the LIFEEZY holds sponges, scrubbers and rags, which suits different habits. If you already own a nice sponge holder, a plain bottle such as the OXO leaves your layout flexible and avoids a caddy that needs wiping.

Manual pumps are cheap, silent and never need power, while touchless units dispense with a wave of the hand. The PZOTRUF 17 Oz uses an infrared sensor with five output levels, which helps when your hands are greasy or when pressing a pump feels like effort. The tradeoff is a power source to monitor and a sensor that can act up with very thick soap. For most kitchens a manual pump like the OXO or the JASAI wins on simplicity, and touchless is worth it only if hands-free matters to you.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kitchen sink fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We read each listing for details that matter at a kitchen sink specifically, not just any counter. That meant looking for dish soap or hand and dish soap use, a spout or pump height that works over a sponge, and a footprint that does not crowd the faucet. The OXO and Casabella scored well here because the listings speak directly to kitchen use. Picks that were only described as bathroom accessories got less credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stability under a wet hand
howWeEvaluated.description: A dispenser that tips when pressed is a daily irritation, so we looked at weight, base design and material. The weighted, non-slip base on the OXO stood out, while glass sets like the COHOSEGE and JASAI rely on their own weight. Plastic caddy units like the LIFEEZY depend more on the counter surface. We treat this as a spec-based assessment, not a measured result.

howWeEvaluated.title: Refill effort and capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared reservoir sizes and opening design, since refilling is the least enjoyable part of owning one. The lineup runs from 13 ounces on the LIFEEZY to 18 ounces on the JASAI, with the PZOTRUF at 17 ounces and the COHOSEGE at 16 ounces. The Casabella earned notes for its pull-tab pump and wide opening. Larger capacity and a wide mouth both lift a pick's score.

howWeEvaluated.title: Durability in a wet room
howWeEvaluated.description: Dish soap dispensers sit in constant moisture, so rust resistance and impact tolerance matter. Stainless steel on the OXO and the 304 pump on the JASAI both help against corrosion, while glass bodies trade durability for visibility. We read buyer feedback themes about leaking pumps, crusted heads and cracked bottles, and weighed them against each listing's materials.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of use and maintenance
howWeEvaluated.description: Last we considered how much effort each pick asks of the owner. A manual pump like the OXO needs nothing beyond occasional wiping, while the PZOTRUF adds a power source and a sensor to watch. Combined units add a caddy to clean. The lineup positions the OXO as the lowest-maintenance pick and the PZOTRUF as the most hands-free, with the others in between.

faq.q: How do I choose between a pump with a caddy and a plain bottle?
faq.a: A caddy unit such as the LIFEEZY or the Casabella Sink Sider Solo suits small sinks, because soap and sponge share one spot. A plain bottle such as the OXO or the JASAI glass gives you more flexibility with your own sponge holder. If counter space is tight, choose the caddy. If you like to swap sponge dishes and keep a clean layout, choose the plain bottle.

faq.q: Is glass or steel better for a kitchen sink?
faq.a: Glass is clearer and prettier, and it shows the remaining soap, which is why the COHOSEGE and JASAI sets appeal to many shoppers. Steel, as on the OXO, is tougher and handles knocks and wet use better. If anyone in the house is careless around the sink, steel or a plastic caddy unit is the safer choice.

faq.q: Are touchless soap dispensers worth it for dish soap?
faq.a: A touchless model like the PZOTRUF 17 Oz can be genuinely helpful when your hands are covered in food, and the five output levels let you tune how much soap comes out. The tradeoff is that it needs power and a working sensor. If you wash dishes with ordinary clean hands, a manual pump is simpler and less likely to cause trouble.

faq.q: How often will I need to refill a dish soap dispenser?
faq.a: That depends on capacity and how much you wash. A 13 ounce LIFEEZY needs topping up sooner than the 18 ounce JASAI bottles. Heavy daily dishwashing means every week or two for small bottles, while light use may stretch to a month. Choose a larger capacity if refilling feels like a chore.

faq.q: Can I use hand soap and dish soap in the same dispenser?
faq.a: Many of these listings say they work with either, including the Casabella and the JASAI bottles. It is better to keep them separate, though, because dish soap and hand soap differ in thickness and scent. That is why the COHOSEGE set includes a labeled pair. If you want only one dispenser, pick the soap you use most.

faq.q: Why does my soap pump stop working or drip?
faq.a: Pumps stall when thick soap dries in the tube, and they drip when soap pools under the head. Rinse the pump with warm water every few weeks and wipe the neck. Thinning very thick soap with a little warm water can help. A steel pump like the one on the JASAI resists corrosion, which reduces sticking over time.

faq.q: How should I clean and maintain a soap dispenser?
faq.a: Wipe the outside with a damp cloth weekly, and every month or so empty it, rinse the bottle, and run warm water through the pump. If your unit has a caddy, like the LIFEEZY, clean where the sponge sits since residue builds there. Replace the sponge regularly, particularly in the Casabella, because a worn sponge holds bacteria and odor.
